html:
A Persian poet and Sufi mystic who lived most of his life in Konya, in Anatolia, and died there in 1273. His long poem the Masnavi is among the most loved poems in the world.

His family came from the region of Balkh, in today's Afghanistan. As the Mongols advanced they fled west, and after years on the road they settled in Konya, capital of the Sultanate of Rum. His name means "the man from Rum", the Muslim name for the old Roman lands of Anatolia. His father was a preacher and scholar, and Rumi followed him as a respected teacher of religious law.

In 1244 he met Shams of Tabriz, a wandering dervish. Their friendship changed him. He turned from law to music, dance and poetry, and when Shams disappeared a few years later his grief poured into thousands of lyric poems, collected as the Divan of Shams.

His great work, the Masnavi, has about 25,000 couplets in six books. It uses stories, jokes and teaching to describe the soul's longing to return to God. Persian readers sometimes call it "the Quran in Persian".

After his death his son organised his followers into the Mevlevi Order, the "whirling dervishes", whose turning dance is a form of prayer. His tomb in Konya is still a place of pilgrimage. He is a central figure of Sufism, and in translation he has become one of the best-selling poets in the United States.
